newsitem.title: UK: Euro refiners see more agony from green rules.
newsitem.headline: Euro refiners see more agony from green rules.

text.p: Europe's ailing oil refineries, reeling from poor returns on investment, face more closures and billions of dollars in fresh costs from tough European Union plans to cut vehicle emissions, industry analysts say.

European Union ministers meeting in Luxembourg last week tightened a draft package of engine emission standards in an effort to more quickly reach air quality objectives in the traffic-choked cities of the group's 15 member states.
Industry analysts say that, if adopted, the new rules are likely to force the hard-pressed European refining sector into a fresh round of closures.
"If we are speaking of one or two (closures), I would not disagree," said Michel Flohic, deputy secretary-general of the European Petroleum Industry Association (EUROPIA).
"The results of the refining industry in Europe have been pretty poor. So by definition to consider additional investment just increases the pressure."
Mike Frend, secretary-general of the UK Petroleum Industry Association (UKPIA) said: "This will force serious consideration of further rationalisation, including possibly closures."

"There is no justification for these limits either in technical terms or in terms of need," Frend added. "The industry made no profit in 1996 and might make no profit in 1997, so where is the investment going to come from?"
"If we shut capacity in Europe then there is the possibility of having to import product, which surely is not in our interests."
The European Parliament is due to give a second reading to the plans in the autumn.
The costs of the new rules would be around $23 billion over 15 years, of which $15 billion would have to be upfront capital investment, EUROPIA said.

The measures toughen previous proposals agreed by the European Commission and which EUROPIA supported. Those measures would have cost the industry only $13 billion overall over 15 years, EUROPIA said, quoting EU figures.

"The Commission's original proposals would have enabled clear air objectives to be achieved. The political views that drove the unnecessary tightening of the fuels proposals do little or nothing for air quality but add 60 percent to 70 percent to the costs," EUROPIA said.

Ministers cut from 200 parts per million to 150 parts per million (ppm) proposed mandatory limits on the sulphur to be allowed in petrol from the year 2000, a move which will curb the damaging effects of sulphur dioxide on catalytic converters fitted to car exhausts.
Ministers also halved benzene levels in petrol to one percent from the year 2000, reducing airborne pollution by the cancer-causing chemical.
They also approved unchanged a proposal to cut sulphur in diesel to 350 parts per million from the current limit of 500 parts per million.
Analysts said the benzene target would cause the industry most pain in terms of technical adjustment, noting the European average at present is 2.3 percent.
Any closures would come on top of years of painful contraction for refiners faced with mounting costs from compliance with ever stricter environmental rules.
EUROPIA says there were 98 refineries in EU member states in 1996 with total capacity of 640 million tonnes, down from 153 refineries with 90 million tonnes in 1980.
But it is not all gloom for the industry.

Some analysts believe new investment triggered by compliance with the rules could raise overall capacity in the EU if refiners follow previous practice and carry out parallel upgrades and de-bottlenecking.
This could be the basis for more gasoline exports to the United States, where tougher specifications have restricted opportunities for EU exports, they said.
Frend said he thought EU ministers were well aware of refiners' low profitability.
But he suggested they were relying on a false perception of oil companies as uniformly rich organisations that could prop up ailing units with cash from more profitable sectors.
He said governments were perfectly well aware that oil companies did not cross-subsidise in that fashion.
